title: A rare case: Spontaneous subdural hematoma in dengue hemorrhagic fever
case_text:
A 52-year-old man came to the emergency room with a sudden loss of consciousness for 1 h. The day prior, the patient had complained of a severe headache with nausea and vomiting more than 5 times. His family denied any other complaints, including seizures, limb weakness, facial drops, and a history of head trauma. This patient had hypertension without any medication. Five days earlier, the patient was hospitalized with DHF. Laboratory findings showed 30,000 thrombocytes and positive immunoglobulin M anti-dengue, and the patient was discharged on the 4th day.
On physical examination, the patient was found to be unresponsive with elevated temperature (38.6 C) and blood pressure (160/90 mmHg). Pulse 102x/min, respiratory rate 24x/min, pulse oximetry 97% on room air. Neurological examination revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 3/15, without signs of meningeal irritation. Anisocoric pupils (6 mm/2 mm) with a negative light reflex were also noted in this patient. Laboratory findings also showed normal blood glucose levels (136 mg/dL), thrombocytopenia (74.000/muL), hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL, hematocrit 41%, normal leukocyte count, coagulation profile, and kidney function. The patient underwent radiological examinations, including a chest X-ray and non-contrast computed tomography (CT) of the head. A mild cardiomegaly was seen in the patient. CT scan showed a wide, hyperdense lesion in the right frontotemporoparietal region extending to the falc cerebri, with a hypodense transition suggestive of a subacute SDH [Figure 1]. Midline shift, a narrowed left ventricle, and cerebral edema were also noted.
Initial management of the patient included intubation with adequate oxygenation. Symptomatic management, mannitol at an initial dose of 200 cc every 8 h, tapering off, ondansetron injection 4 mg every 12 h, followed by citicoline mecobalamin injection. Antibiotics, ceftriaxone injection, were also given every 12 h. The patient underwent treatment in the intensive care unit under close monitoring, with no surgical intervention. Despite intensive medical therapy, the patient's condition worsened within 2 days of treatment, with signs of brainstem herniation. His pupils remained anisocor and unresponsive to light, and his blood pressure gradually decreased. The patient had a cardiac arrest on the 3rd day of treatment.
